name: adopt_repository
description:
Adopt an existing GitHub repository as a project's remote, by its real name.

`run_devops_setup`'s repository step derives the name it looks for from the
project's own display name — lowercase, non-alphanumeric runs collapsed to
a single dash — and only reaches the adopt-vs-create decision once a repo
of that exact derived name is found. A real repo named any other way
(underscores, or a different word entirely) is a lookup miss, not a
collision: setup would silently create a second, empty, unrelated
repository and push the current working tree into it, never considering
the real one.

This runs the same repository step by the repository's own real name
instead of a guessed one, so it reaches the real repo directly and adopts
it — same push-and-prove behavior `run_devops_setup` would otherwise do,
just aimed correctly.

## `owner` is the other half of "the real repo"

A name alone still is not enough when the repository lives in an
organisation rather than the connected account's own login.
`Repository.ensure/3` looks up `owner || authenticated_owner(scope)` — the
authenticated user's own account — when nothing else is said, and this
tool had no way to say otherwise. Found live: a project whose real
repository is `Code-My-Spec/broken-oaths` adopted `johns10/broken-oaths`
instead — a *different*, genuinely existing repository that happened to
share the name under the account the OAuth token authenticates as — and
failed the push with "origin already points at
https://github.com/Code-My-Spec/broken-oaths.git, not
https://github.com/johns10/broken-oaths.git", which reads as the wrong
repository having been *found*, not as a parameter that was silently never
offered. `owner` here is passed straight through as `Repository.ensure/3`'s
own `:owner` opt, which already worked for both a personal account and an
organisation login — the gap was only ever this tool's schema.

`push/3`'s default branch is `"main"`, which the repository step never
overrides — a real checkout whose default branch is anything else (a
pre-existing `master`, for instance) would push nothing, since `git push
origin main` has no local `main` to push. Safe (it fails cleanly rather
than pushing the wrong content), but still a step that would otherwise
fail for no reason a caller could see, so this exposes the same override
`push/3` already supports.

Only pushes what is already committed — `ensure_commit/1` stages and
commits only when the checkout has no commit at all yet, and the one other
commit this can make (`commit_owner_patch/1`) touches only the generated CI
workflow file, explicitly, never a broad `add -A`. Uncommitted local
changes and untracked files in the working tree are not staged, committed,
or pushed as a side effect of adopting.

## Returns when the run starts, not when it finishes

A push is normally seconds, but a slow network, a large repository, or
GitHub itself can run this well past the code-mode sandbox's 30s wall
clock (issue 4f7929e4) — this used to hold `RunLock` and wait for the real
push inline, on the stated bet that "a push is seconds, not minutes",
which is a considered bet, not a guarantee. The spawned task claims this
project's own lock and only then acks, the same handshake
`run_provisioning_step` uses: the reply is "started" or "already running";
an agent that started it is messaged the outcome, any other caller watches
`devops_status`.

branch.description: The checkout's actual default branch, if it isn't "main" (e.g. "master").

owner.description: The account or organisation the repository actually lives under, if it is not the connected account's own login (e.g. "Code-My-Spec").

repository_name.description: The GitHub repository's exact name, e.g. "market_my_spec" — not a guess.

name: devops_status
description:
Whether the infrastructure this account is supposed to have actually exists.

Answers three separate questions, because conflating them is what made
"is devops setup done?" unanswerable:

- **missing** — a step whose resources are not there. This is what decides
  whether `devops_setup` is complete.
- **dangling** — a resource that exists and points at nothing, usually a DNS
  record left over from a destroyed server. Not a completion problem; it is
  cleanup, and it does not block the requirement.
- **unreachable** — a provider that could not be read. This is the absence of
  an answer, not a verdict. Do not treat it as "not done".

Read from the providers, not from a record file. Setup completion used to be
decided by grepping a markdown file for the words "verified" and "prod",
which an agent could satisfy by writing prose.

## Never sees past the one project it is connected to

`Resources.report/1` is deliberately account-wide — the cross-project
dangling checks need to see everything, and that is right for `/app/
resources`, a human looking at their own whole account. It is wrong for
this tool: a caller reaching it through the harness is scoped to one
project's work, and has no business learning what devops state, missing
steps, or dangling resources some *other* project in the same account
carries. Confirmed live, twice: first a project whose own devops was
still `:off` got back a different project's checklist entirely; then,
once devops was turned on, that *same* other project kept appearing in
full detail beside the real answer, because the underlying call was still
`Resources.report/1`. This uses `Resources.project_report/2` instead,
which never runs `deployable/1` or asks a provider for anything beyond
the one project it is given — there is no account-wide data left to leak,
on or off.

name: ensure_environment
description:
Create or update a durable environment for this project.
Choose management "harness" for a destination run by a connected device,
such as local development, or "provisioned" for a provider-managed deployment,
such as UAT or production. Defaults to "provisioned" for existing callers.
An existing environment's management cannot be changed. This does not
provision infrastructure or start an app. Use list_environments to inspect
destinations and assign_app_instance_environment to bind an app instance.

management.description: How this destination is managed; defaults to provisioned.

name: ensure_server_access_key
description:
The account's SSH public key, minted if it doesn't exist yet.

For a box CodeMySpec creates itself, `Servers.access_key/1` uploads this
key to the provider as part of creation and nothing else is needed. For a
box the account already owned before linking it — the case this tool is
for — there is no provider API that retrofits an SSH key onto an
already-existing server. The account owner adds this text to that box's
`authorized_keys` once, by hand; after that, every project's server step
reaches it the same way it reaches a box CodeMySpec built from scratch.

Only the public key is ever returned. The private half stays in
`AccountSecrets` and never leaves the server.

name: generate_deploy_files
description:
Write the deploy artifacts a project is missing, onto its own checkout.

The same write `ProvisioningLive`'s "Generate deploy files" button performs
— `DeployArtifacts.generate/2`, which never overwrites a file already there.
Exists as its own tool, not folded into `run_devops_setup`, because it is not
an ordered step: nothing in the sequence runs it, `devops_status`'s
deploy-readiness audit only reads what it should have produced, and an agent
that has just read "missing lib/<app>/release.ex" from that audit needs a way
to put it there without a browser.

Writes onto the checkout of whichever project this call is connected to —
no `project_id` parameter, so there is nothing for a caller to name (or
mis-name) a different project's tree with.

name: import_age_key
description:
Record an environment's age key when it was generated on a real checkout
this server cannot reach, rather than minted here.

`.sops.yaml` and an environment's `envs/*.enc.env` are files that live in
and get committed to a project's own working tree — real local-filesystem
work, the same category as `:repository`'s git push, and just as
unreachable through the light harness for a project with no checkout on
this side. When that local work happens somewhere that *does* have a real
checkout instead (a developer's own machine, a harness with a live
registration), the private half of the key it generated still has to land
here — or the next thing on this side that needs to decrypt (`:deploy`,
another secret write) mints a *different* key under the same name, and
every ciphertext already committed under the real one becomes unreadable
to it.

private_key.description: The environment's private age key (AGE-SECRET-KEY-...), as generated by age-keygen.

name: link_server
description:
Legacy provider-name convenience for binding a provisioned environment to
an account's existing provider device. Use list_devices and
assign_environment_device for canonical UUID-based placement, including
harness-managed environments. Provider devices are managed under /app/devices.

The named server must already be linked to this account. Creates the
provisioned environment if needed. This only changes its device binding;
it does not move or deploy app instances or working copies.

server_name.description: Name of a server already linked to this account, e.g. "fuellytics-prod".

name: provider_request
description:
Make an arbitrary Hetzner, Cloudflare or Resend API call on the agent's
behalf, without the agent ever holding the credential.

`Hetzner`/`Cloudflare`/`Resend` each already resolve their own credential
server-side and make the authenticated call — that's the same "agent asks,
server acts" shape every other provisioning tool here already uses. This
is that plumbing, generalized: the fixed provisioning-step tools
(`run_devops_setup`, `ensure_environment`, ...) cover the sequence; this
covers everything that doesn't fit the sequence — inspecting what's
already on a shared box before adopting it, attaching a firewall to a
server that already exists, confirming something reached the provider at
all.

Reads are unrestricted. A mutating method (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) without
`confirm: true` is refused outright — this exists to make destructive
action against a real account deliberate, not a thing an agent can do by
constructing the wrong path on a whim. Every mutating call, confirmed or
refused, is logged with enough detail to reconstruct what happened and why.

body.description: JSON body for a mutating request.

confirm.description: Required (true) for POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE. Ignored for GET.

method.description: HTTP method: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE.

params.description: Query parameters for a GET request.

path.description: Path relative to the provider's API base, e.g. "/servers" or "/zones".

name: provision_account_server
description:
Bring up (or adopt) one account-owned server: the box itself, its shared
registry container, and its shared database container — ready for any
project to link an environment onto afterward.

This is the account-level half of the hard line stories 989/990 drew:
server and box-wide container creation live here, never in a project's own
devops step (`run_provisioning_step`/`run_devops_setup`), which refuses to
reach `Hetzner.create_server` under any circumstance
(`Steps.server_creation_gate/3`). Once this tool has run, a project points
an environment at the result with `link_server` — this tool never touches a
project or an environment itself.

Idempotent both ways — a name the provider already has is adopted, not
duplicated (`Hetzner.ensure_server/3`), and a name this account has already
linked keeps its machine identity. A conflicting provider resource ID is refused. Safe to
call again for a box whose registry or database came up short the first
time; both container checks start from "is this already true" before doing
anything.

## Returns when the run starts, not when it finishes

Creating a box, waiting for it to boot over SSH, and checking its registry
and database containers can run well past the code-mode sandbox's 30s wall
clock (issue 4f7929e4) — this used to call `Steps.provision_account_server/3`
synchronously and risk a `:brutal_kill` mid-creation, with no cleanup able
to run. The name is still linked synchronously, so a caller can trust it is
on file the moment this returns; then a spawned task claims this account's
own lock and only then acks, the same handshake `run_provisioning_step`
uses. The reply is "started" or "already running"; an agent that started it
is messaged the outcome, any other caller calls this tool again to check.

The lock is the ACCOUNT's, not a project's: the box, its registry and its
database are shared by every project the account has, so two projects
racing to provision the same account's server must share one lock rather
than each getting their own and racing the provider directly.

## Not yet restricted by identity

Nothing today restricts *who* may call this the way `server_creation_gate`
restricts what a project-scoped step may do. A dedicated account-level
agent — with its own tool set excluding this from every project-scoped
caller structurally, not just by convention — was part of the original
design for this split and was cut from this round of work as unnecessary
scope. Until something like it exists, this tool is reachable the same way
every other devops tool is: by whatever session is connected, through code
mode. The refusal that actually matters — no project-scoped path reaches
create-server — holds regardless, enforced in `Steps.ex` itself rather than
by who is allowed to call this tool.

name.description: The server's name at the provider — an existing box to adopt as the account's, or a new one to create under this name.

name: query_telemetry
description:
Read back the calling project's own collected logs and traces.

Scoped to the project the call resolves to -- never another project's,
even when two projects share a telemetry host on the same server. That
isolation is `CodeMySpec.Telemetry.query/3`'s own contract; this tool
only adapts the MCP params into it.

since_days.description: How many days back to read. Defaults to the retention window (14 days) -- nothing older could have survived it anyway.

name: read_database_url
description:
The connection string `:server` already minted for this environment's
database.

`Database.serve/3` mints and stores this project's role/database
credential in `ProjectSecrets` the moment it provisions the container and
tenant — before the step ever reaches the part that writes it into
`envs/*.enc.env`, which is real local-filesystem work a project with no
checkout on this side cannot complete (the same wall `:repository` hits).
This is the read half of that gap: the credential already exists, and a
caller with a real checkout elsewhere needs the value itself to encrypt it
there, rather than this server minting it a second time somewhere it
cannot commit anything.

## The value is unverified

This reads `ProjectSecrets` alone — it does not check that the role or
database the credential names still exists on the box. `serve/3`'s own
`sync_password/2` runs unconditionally on every `:server` step, so "run
:server, then read this" is always current; read on its own after the box
has been touched independently (recreated, restored, migrated to a new
server) can hand back a credential for a tenant that no longer exists,
with nothing here to say so.

name: read_project_file
description:
Read a file from a project's own checkout.

Read-only counterpart to `generate_deploy_files`. `devops_status`'s audit can
say a file is misconfigured (`force_ssl` without a health exclusion, say) but
never shows the content — and `DeployArtifacts.generate/2` deliberately never
overwrites a file that already exists, so a misconfigured (as opposed to
missing) artifact has no automated fix. Seeing the real content is the step
before deciding how to fix it by hand.

path.description: Path relative to the project root.

name: read_registry_credential
description:
The self-hosted registry's address, image path, and credential for this
project.

`:server` already minted and stored this project's registry credential in
`ProjectSecrets` (`Registry.credential/1`) the moment it provisioned the
registry container. A caller with a real checkout this server cannot reach
— updating a hand-written `config/deploy.yml` to point at the self-hosted
registry instead of ghcr.io, or logging in to push/pull by hand — needs
the actual values, not a second credential minted somewhere it could never
commit a config change to use it.

## The address is per environment, not per project

Two environments can live on two different boxes with two different real
registry addresses — `Registry.default_host/0`'s "localhost:5000" is only
ever right for a registry bound to loopback, not true of a shared box's
container today. `environment` resolves the same way
`DeployArtifacts`/`ProvisioningLive`'s own generated configs do
(`Steps.registry_address/3`: this server's own adopted network, never one
derived from the project's name), so the address is real rather than a
project-wide placeholder.

name: run_devops_setup
description:
Build the infrastructure that is missing, for the project this call is
connected to.

This provisions **real resources in real accounts** — servers, DNS records,
buckets, sending domains — and they cost money and change where mail and
traffic go. It is the same run the provisioning page's per-project button
performs.

No `project_id` parameter, on purpose. This used to take one, and
separately accepted omitting it entirely as a bulk "build every project
whose devops level is not off" mode — either shape let a caller name (or
fail to name) a *different* project than the one this call is actually
connected to, sometimes triggering real, costed provisioning on projects
nobody asked to touch. Found during an audit prompted by a real,
unrelated cross-project leak in `devops_status`. The only project this
tool can ever act on now is `Validators.devops_project/1`'s answer —
whichever project the connection itself identifies (the harness's own
`X-Project-ID` header, or the configured project for stdio) — the same
fix applied to every other devops tool.

The sequence is ordered and halts on the first failure, which is deliberate —
the ordering *is* the dependency model. A step that pauses is waiting on a
decision only a person can make (a credential that cannot be minted through
an API, an apex that is already serving a live site); read what it says
rather than retrying it.

Call `devops_status` first. If it reports a provider unreachable, the answer
is unknown rather than "not done", and running setup on that basis may build
things that already exist.

## This returns as soon as the run starts, not when it finishes

A real run can take minutes — deploy alone has measured ~167s — which is
longer than this tool's own transport waits for a reply. Calling and then
waiting for a definitive "complete" here will time out even when the run is
proceeding normally; call `devops_status` afterward to watch it converge
instead of retrying this call. Retrying while a run is still going does not
start a second one — the project is locked for the run's duration and the
retry is told a run is already in progress, rather than racing the first
run's writes against the same provider.

An agent that started the run is messaged how it ended instead, and is not
nudged meanwhile (`Starter`, `Agents.Waiting`).

name: run_provisioning_step
description:
Run one named provisioning step directly, skipping the sequence's own
halt-on-first-failure ordering.

`run_devops_setup` walks `Sequence.for_options/1` in order and halts at the
first step that is not done. That stops being useful when an earlier step is
blocked for a reason unrelated to later ones — `:repository` and `:secrets`
need a local checkout the light harness cannot provide, while provider-API
steps (`:server`, `:domain`, `:dns`, …) can still be verified. This bypasses
ordering only: the step is the same `Provisioning.run_step/3`, verified
against the provider first, under the same `RunLock`, and a step that cannot
run yet is still that step's to refuse.

## Confirmations an agent can give

`inbound_probe_to`, `confirm_apex_repoint` and `confirm_inbound_mx_repoint`
carry the answers a step pauses for, so an agent with no person at the
console can supply them. `:server` never creates a server here: an unlinked
environment's step always pauses; only `Steps.provision_account_server/3`,
through the account-level tool, creates one.

## Returns when the step starts, not when it finishes

A step can outlive the caller's transport and the code-mode sandbox's 30s
wall clock (`:deploy` takes minutes). The spawned task claims `RunLock` and
only then acks, so the reply is "started" or "already running". An agent
that started the step is messaged its outcome; any other caller watches
`devops_status`.

See knowledge/tools, "run_provisioning_step".

confirm_apex_repoint.description: For the "dns" step only: the apex already resolves somewhere, and this run would repoint it at a server it just created — which takes down whatever is live there today. The step pauses and names the current and new address instead of doing this silently; set this to true once that repoint is actually wanted, and call the step again.

confirm_inbound_mx_repoint.description: For the "inbound" step only: the domain already has an MX record, and publishing Resend's here would replace rather than add to it — which can silently redirect or break mail that already routes through the existing one. The step pauses and names the current record instead of doing this silently; set this to true once that replacement is actually wanted, and call the step again.

environment.description: Required for the "deploy" step: which environment to deploy (e.g. "uat"). Deploying is a decision about one specific environment, not a batch operation — without this, `Steps.run(:deploy, …)` would deploy every environment the project has in one call, in an unspecified order, stopping at the first failure. That silently includes prod even when a caller only meant to touch uat, so this tool requires naming the one environment intended.

force.description: Skip verification and run the step unconditionally, even if the provider already reports it satisfied. A step's own claim of "satisfied" can be narrower than everything its run actually does — e.g. "server" only checks the box and DATABASE_URL exist, not that the box's docker daemon trusts the registry it should. Every step's run is idempotent, so this is safe to use whenever a step reports done but something it should have set up still isn't.

inbound_probe_to.description: For the "inbound" step only: an address on the project's own domain to prove receiving works (e.g. "sam@example.com"). Resend accepts mail only to addresses configured for the domain, so this cannot be guessed.

step.description: One of: repository, server, secrets, domain, dns, tls, deploy, email, inbound, storage, backups, content, widget, callback_credential, monitoring, telemetry.

telemetry_mode.description: For the "telemetry" step only: "full" (the default: ClickHouse and the collector), "capped" (ClickHouse with a memory cap) or "collector_only" (only the OTLP collector; data queues locally until ClickHouse is installed). Pick capped or collector_only on a box shared with other apps.

name: save_provider_credential
description:
Save one provider credential — a Hetzner, Cloudflare or Resend API key —
on the agent's behalf.

For the case `ProviderRequest`'s own "agent asks, server acts" shape
doesn't cover: an agent that has *obtained* a credential (from the
person it's working with, from a setup wizard elsewhere) and needs it on
file before the provisioning steps that read it can run. The value is
written straight through to `Credentials.put_value/3` — the same write
the console's own credentials form makes — and never echoed back.

name: write_project_file
description:
Overwrite a file in a project's own checkout.

`DeployArtifacts.generate/2` deliberately never touches a file that already
exists — a project that customised its Dockerfile did so for a reason. That
is right for *scaffolding* a missing artifact and wrong for *fixing* one
`devops_status`'s audit has already named as misconfigured (`force_ssl`
without a health exclusion, say): there, the file exists, is wrong, and
regenerating from the template would silently discard whatever else the
project put there. This is the deliberate, explicit override for that case —
read the real content with `read_project_file` first, change only what needs
changing, and write the whole file back.

content.description: Full file content — this replaces whatever is there.

path.description: Path relative to the project root.
